<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and stayed on the stated motion, but B built a tighter causal mechanism (expectations formation, lagging indicators) that survived the exchange better than A's framework. When pressed for an operational trigger for abandoning patience, A offered a concrete two-quarter/expectations rule in Rebuttal 2 — but B's follow-up (B4.1/B5.1) turned that answer against A, showing that by the time such a trigger fires, wage contracts and pricing decisions are already locked in on the assumption of drift, meaning "patience" doesn't avoid the recession, it just delays and enlarges it. A never directly neutralized this specific mechanism in the closing, instead re-asserting uncertainty symmetry and burden-of-proof framing without engaging the "lagging by construction" point. A's strongest moves (recession scarring is not fully reversible, uncertainty cuts against aggressive tightening too, extra speed must be justified) were live and reasonably answered by B's "neither path is costless, but only one compounds without a stopping mechanism" framing. Overall B's case cohered into a single decisive comparative claim ("arithmetic": smaller/bounded cost now vs. larger/guaranteed cost later) that A's closing did not fully dismantle, giving B a clear, if not overwhelming, edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 / Closing exploitation of A's own proposed trigger (A4.1) — arguing that any threshold detecting entrenched expectations necessarily fires only after wage/price contracts already reflect the drift, so A's "conditional patience" cannot actually prevent the recession it hopes to avoid, only postpone and enlarge it. A's closing did not squarely answer this.</best_rebuttal>
